Task: Write a quick note explaining why TCP differs from UDP.

Quick note:  
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) and UDP (User Datagram Protocol) both run on top of IP, but they serve different needs. TCP is connection-oriented: before any data is exchanged, the two endpoints perform a three-way handshake to establish a reliable connection. Once connected, TCP guarantees that packets arrive intact, in order, and without duplication, using acknowledgments, sequence numbers, retransmissions, and congestion control. All of this adds latency and overhead but provides reliability. UDP, by contrast, is connection-less and adds almost no extra features beyond basic checksums for error detection. There is no handshake, acknowledgments, or built-in retransmission, so packets may be lost, duplicated, or arrive out of order. This makes UDP faster and better suited to applications that can tolerate some loss and need low latency—such as real-time audio/video or online gaming—while TCP is preferred when accuracy and completeness of data are critical, such as file transfers or web traffic.
